text: FLEX maps flammability boundaries for burning liquid-fuel droplets in reduced gravity and measures how effective gaseous suppressants are across candidate pressures and oxygen levels.

FLEX test variables: oxygen mole fraction 0.10 to 0.50, pressure 0.5 to 1.0 atm, carbon dioxide and helium suppressants up to about 0.70 mole fraction, methanol and heptane fuels, droplets of 2 to 5 mm.
Low-pressure suppressant data matters because one fire strategy is to isolate a habitat and vent the cabin to space.
FLEX-2 studies sub-buoyant convective flow, droplet pairs and bi-component or surrogate fuels, in groups of roughly 30 to 60 tests.

BASS burned 41 solid samples (flat, spheres, candles in tubes) in the Microgravity Science Glovebox using a fan-driven duct with airflow set from 5 to 50 cm/s and nitrogen supplied from 0 to 500 cc/min until extinction.
BASS tests whether materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation burn as well as or better than in normal gravity under identical pressure, oxygen and temperature.
In microgravity the best point to apply a suppressant may not be obvious, and a stream could make a flame worse by entraining oxygen.
BASS-II used 100 samples and varied ambient oxygen, ventilation flow, and fuel type, thickness and geometry; models predicted higher flame spread rates than were observed.
NASA screens spacecraft materials with the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 upward-burning test in normal gravity, which may not capture low-gravity behavior.
A Moon base or pressurized rover atmosphere is expected to have oxygen of about 30% or more at 10.2 psi or less, which makes materials much more flammable than in Earth air.
No partial-gravity combustion data is currently in PSI; LUCI and FM2 may add some. Microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound intermediate gravity levels.
SAME and SAME-R tested smoke detection in microgravity; the DAFT studies reused one of the instruments to detect dust.
Solid-material flammability was studied in BASS, BASS-II and Saffire; suppression of liquid droplets was studied in FLEX by diluting the atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium.
